World.title: Female veterans find solace in surf with 'life-changing' therapy
World.content:
As dawn breaks over Mudjimba Beach, on Queensland's Sunshine Coast, a woman rallies the troops for their morning mission.

They are armed with surfboards and there is a nervous energy in the crisp autumn air.

Tammy Grant speaks to groups of women as part of the surf therapy program. (Supplied: Matt Pope Photography)

Most of the women have just met, and the ocean did not get the memo that a bunch of beginners was about to hit the waves.

"The surf on day one was massive, like six to eight feet, and I was like, 'Oh my God, how am I going to host this?'," Tammy Grant said.

Ms Grant, the event organiser, soldiered on knowing that if anyone could handle a challenge it would be a group of female veterans.

Surf therapy combines surfing with mental health support to improve psychological, physical and social wellbeing. (Supplied: Matt Pope Photography)

"We ended up getting them out on the boards and in the whitewash," Ms Grant said.

"Just to see the very same people who were so depressed just two hours earlier have these massive smiles … let go of the 'strong girl' facade and enjoy the moment with a bunch of other bad-ass women — it was incredible."

The group quickly embraced the challenging surf conditions. (Supplied: Matt Pope Photography)

'I'd felt nothing'

The surf therapy retreat, believed to be the first of its kind in Australia tailored specifically for female veterans, was held in March.

Tammy Grant plans to run more retreats to help female veterans. (Supplied: Tammy Grant)

Ms Grant spent 14 years in the defence force, and the next seven years trying to recover from her experience.

"I came from quite a traumatic childhood, then I went on to join the army when I was about 19 years old, experiencing my first deployment to Afghanistan when I was 22, so it's a bit of a shock," she said.

Having initially served as a transport operator, she then became a nursing officer.

"I got diagnosed with PTSD as a result of my childhood, stuff that's happened in my service in terms of deployment, and some sexual assault kind of stuff," she said.

She tried all kinds of therapies until she finally found solace in the surf, through the Waves of Wellness program.

"When I was out in the water, I could feel my body responding — I could feel alive," she said.

" I felt amazing when, the last six, seven years I'd felt just … nothing. "

The first group of veterans to take part in the course have described it as life-changing. (Supplied: Matt Pope Photography)

Ms Grant decided to do a deeper dive into the program, studying for a postgraduate degree in mental health and neuroscience.

She also went to Scotland last year for the International Surf Therapy Organization's inaugural global conference and "just sponged everything up".

"I decided this is the perfect blend of all my skills that I have developed and my life experiences," she said, adding that she was also collaborating with the Women Veterans SURF Project in the US, with the aim to raise awareness globally.

Several local female coaches came on board to teach participants how to surf. (Supplied: Matt Pope Photography)

Struggles of civilian life

Hannah Jagger, who was medically retired after spending 10 years as an army medic, said she was initially hesitant to join the retreat to help with her PTSD.

"My psychologist actually pushed me to go," Ms Jagger said.

" I was pretty stand-offish day one. I really struggled. I think day two everybody kind of opened up and then the flow started. "

Hannah Jagger said it was refreshing to meet other like-minded women at the retreat. (Supplied: Matt Pope Photography)

Ms Jagger travelled up from New South Wales.

"When we leave the military, we lose those friendships and people that just get you," she said.

"We are expected to go back into everyday civilian life and become an everyday person and it's really challenging."

She described the experience as "life-changing" and was so inspired she has now come on board as a sponsor to enable Ms Grant to offer subsidised enrolments for future programs.

Hannah Jagger said the women have all become "beautiful friends". (Supplied: Tammy Grant)

A different battle

Lee Feakes joined the defence force later in life, serving as a technician for a decade.

"I was like a dog with two tails when I first joined the military. I was 45. This is what I want to do with my life," Ms Feakes said.

"I loved every day — until I didn't.

"Being bullied, sexually harassed, assaulted, it ruined the whole experience for me."

Lee Feakes feels being in the ocean for the therapy is less intimidating. (Supplied: Matt Pope Photography)

She said she tried everything to get past her PTSD, but most veteran programs were geared towards men.

"I've done programs with males and I have had to change the way I speak, withhold information, because I know it would start something," she said.

Ms Feakes said being in the ocean instead of a "clinical" environment with a therapist also felt less intimidating.

"If you're in a group and you don't feel like sharing today, that's OK," she said.

" When you're out in the ocean on a surfboard, it's complete mindfulness because you can only think about what you're doing and suddenly your brain is in relaxed mode. "

Lee Feakes said it was amazing to see the transformation in the women during the retreat. (Supplied: Matt Pope Photography)

Not all trauma from combat

Lyndsay Free, board director of Women Veterans Australia, said many women found leaving the defence force a "big and confronting adjustment" as they also navigated caregiving, parenting and relationship pressures.

"Current statistics show that former-serving women veterans are more than twice as likely to die by suicide as Australian civilian women," Ms Free said.

"We need to stop pretending all veteran trauma comes from combat. For some women, the deepest trauma came from experiences within the system itself.

Lyndsay Free says women veterans have added pressures when it comes to transitioning back into civilian life. (Supplied: Women Veterans Australia)

"Military sexual trauma is an uncomfortable conversation, but an essential one if we're serious about veteran wellbeing.

"PTSD doesn't care whether your trauma came from deployment, assault, chronic exposure to stress, or a combination of all three — trauma is trauma."

She commended Ms Grant on her program, which would help women who might otherwise "suffer in silence".

Tammy Grant plans to run another female veterans retreat in November. (Supplied: Matt Pope Photography)

"Women veterans aren't a niche subset of the community," Ms Free said.

" We're more than 125,000 Australians who've served, yet veteran programs can't effectively support people they still struggle to properly see. "

World.title: Could a roof sprinkler save your home in a bushfire?
World.content:
Three small flecks, barely perceptible, scar the front deck of Ivan and Pam Walker's Tasmanian home.

Left by embers, they are the home's only signs of a bushfire that five months earlier raged through the east coast town of Stieglitz.

"It will always be a memory of how lucky we were, really," Ms Walker said.

Ivan and Pam Walker say the effort and investment in preparing their home against bushfire has paid off. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Over the fence, blackened tree trunks — their canopies burnt red — protrude from scorched earth.

The eerie scene is a sobering reminder of how different things could have been for the Walkers.

"We're unscathed and right beside there's a house gone, and there wasn't even a fence post burnt on our place," Mr Walker said.

Ivan Walker says "there wasn't even a fence post burnt on our place". (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

A fire-resilient home

In December, what started as a residential fire pit at nearby Dianas Basin quickly burned through more than 1,200 hectares, destroying two homes.

The Walkers will never forget the glow of the flames through the trees, the dark clouds, and the distressed call of birds as the inferno crept closer.

It was the moment they would put their bushfire preparations to the test.

Hundreds of residents living near Dianas Basin were evacuated from their homes late last year. (Supplied: Michael Hoult)

Adamant about making their home as fire-resistant as possible, the couple were deliberate in their design and material choices, getting as granular as the window lining.

They installed a rooftop sprinkler system, rigging up four irrigation sprayers to a steel water tank powered by a pump.

And they were religious about maintaining their firebreak.

"You've got to respect fire," Mr Walker said.

The Stieglitz bushfire burned through more than 1,200 hectares of bushland, and destroyed two houses. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Running on adrenaline as they executed their fire plan, they turned on the sprinkler system once the fire reached their back fence, hoped for the best, then drove off.

They later pulled up to a nearby beach to watch.

"And that's when the reality really sank in that we may lose our property," Ms Walker said.

"The fire was just exploding. The pine trees in our neighbour's property were just going 'whoosh' up into the sky, and our house was right beside that.

"And we're thinking, 'oh my gosh, are we going to have a house?'.

"We took all the precautions we could, but just not knowing was pretty scary."

The bushfire ravaged the community in the weeks leading up to Christmas. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

'Surreal' to see house standing

Although they had been assured by firefighters that their home was still standing, the Walkers were in disbelief when they returned days later.

"It was just surreal to see that the house was still here and amazement that there was just no damage," Ms Walker said.

The December bushfire burned up to the perimeter fence of the Walker's home. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Local plumber and volunteer firefighter Paul Fisher installed the sprinkler system and helped protect the home from the blaze.

He said the sprinklers, aided by more benign winds, helped fight off the fire.

"It just creates a curtain of water around the place and around the perimeter," he said.

"It was a fairly basic system on that house, but it did make a lot of difference and wetted down the house and all the surrounding structures and decks."

Paul Fisher installed the rooftop sprinklers on the Walkers' home. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

Since the fire, Mr Fisher has received a slight uptick in people enquiring about similar set-ups.

"That's good. It's never too late," he said.

" Anything's better than nothing. "

Improved building regulations have resulted in Australian homes with an 80-per-cent chance of withstanding a bushfire. (Supplied: April Bosworth)

Have you thought about the doormat?

Australia's fire seasons are becoming longer and more extreme, and while it is impossible to make homes entirely fireproof, preparation can go a long way.

Recently retired CSIRO scientist Justin Leonard has spent a career focused on the bushfire risk to Australian homes.

He said good design was important, and features such as sprinkler systems helped, as part of a holistic approach.

"Making your house resilient is all about getting that full list of ways the bushfire could find little nooks and crannies, or exploit a particular thing like a doormat, and to work through that entire list," he said.

"It's only once you've solved the last of that long list of weak links that the house is going to then be a really, really good performer in a bushfire."

Justin Leonard says some home insurers provide policy discounts for home owners who take steps to reduce their house's bushfire risk. (ABC News: Marty McCarthy)

He said embers had an "uncanny ability" to find flammable debris hiding in places such as the ledge of a timber window, or a gap between roof tiles.

"And those ignitions in the building cavities or under your deck, or under your floor space then develop and almost certainly take out your house," he said.

Homes on the frontline of a bushfire historically had a survival rate of about 60 per cent, but Mr Leonard said improved building regulations pushed that figure to around 80 per cent.

But he said regulations were a "minimum safety net", and further efforts could extend a home's bushfire survivability rate to above 90 per cent, or closer to 100 per cent.

He acknowledged that cost could be a barrier, but said many of the measures — such as a rainwater tank or a solar panel-powered battery — could also reduce water and electricity bills.

How to plant fire-smart gardens Scientists say garden beds can act as a line of defence against bushfires.

While in its infancy, some insurers provide discounts for home improvements that reduce bushfire risk.

"Formalising the way you build a checklist and work through it and prove that to your insurer is starting to become a really important way to … solve that monetary issue," Mr Leonard said.

For the Walkers, the effort and investment have paid off.

"We've had a lot of questions and 'oh that's your house that survived', 'you were so lucky' and 'it was just an act of God' and we said, 'we were prepared'," Mr Walker said.

World.title: F1 driver smashes into groundhog during Canadian Grand Prix session
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli led George Russell to a Mercedes one-two in a practice session at the Canadian Grand Prix that was interrupted after Alex Albon's Williams hit a groundhog.

Warning: The vision below may be upsetting to some readers.

Albon crashed heavily when he was unable to avoid the animal on the exit of turn seven. Albon slid down the barriers for some distance on the straight that follows the corner, causing heavy damage to his car.

The red flag caused by the incident was one of three: the first when Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson stopped on track with a loss of steering caused by a hydraulics leak, and the final one when Esteban Ocon crashed his Haas after spinning on the exit of turn four.

Russell later bounced back after a difficult recent run to beat Antonelli to sprint pole.

Russell, who is 20 points adrift of the Italian after four races this season, headed Antonelli by 0.068 seconds after being fastest on both runs in final qualifying.

Lando Norris headed an all-McLaren second row, 0.315secs off pole and 0.019secs in front of teammate Oscar Piastri.

'One of the risks of this circuit'

There have been a number of incidents where drivers have collided with groundhogs at the Canadian Grand Prix, including one last year involving Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari.

Groundhogs, a type of large ground squirrel native to North America, are commonplace around the track in Montreal, which is on an artificial island in the Saint Lawrence River.

"It's one of the risks of this circuit. I know that sounds strange," Williams team principal James Vowles told Sky Sports.

"Unfortunately there's been a few of these.

"He [Albon] has hit a marmot [groundhog] and the damage is extensive from that point onwards.

"He needed this session. You get 60 minutes and that's it, and to lose over half of it is frustrating.

"Back in the garage he's more worried about his mum, who suspects he's going to have to pay to adopt a family of marmots because that's a consequence of that."

ABC Sport will be live blogging all the action from the Canadian Grand Prix on Monday from 5am (AEST).

World.title: Albany's hidden WWII fuel tanks transformed into global street art gallery
World.content:
Tucked away in bushland on Western Australia's south coast, a World War II relic has been brought back to life as a sprawling gallery for street artists.

The towering concrete walls of seven abandoned wartime fuel tanks just outside Albany are drawing creatives from all over the world.

In turn, these artists are helping to shine a spotlight on a once-vital site that was shrouded in secrecy.

The towering walls of the tanks create an echo chamber. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

"It was somewhere that was forgotten about, left to just go to waste, and we just reclaimed it really," local artist Chad Marwick said.

"And then the history of the place itself gets talked about as well."

The tanks attract admiring visitors. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

Marwick said the tanks included work from artists from near and far.

"You get people who just love to travel, you know, from all over Australia, even international artists have been in there," he said.

Art and history

The decommissioned tanks were once vital wartime infrastructure in the Great Southern city.

Part of the immersive experience of the tanks is the way the art interplays with the natural light. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

Local historian Malcolm Traill said censorship during the war meant very little information about the tanks was shared publicly, even though they loomed out of the bush.

"They're a reminder of that time more than 80 years ago during World War II," he said.

The tanks were once under threat of demolition, but local advocates fought to preserve them because of their historical significance.

The work ranges from intricate stencils to more traditionally styled pieces. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

The street art is now also helping increase public awareness about the site, which Mr Traill says is a "good thing".

The art reflects off the surface of large pools of water inside the tanks. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

"Street art is a modern phenomenon and I think it brightens things up," he said.

"Grey concrete is not the most exciting thing to look at.

" If it brings people in and gets that story out there, then it's got to be a good thing. "

Documenting the past

In addition to the street art, community organisation Veterans Assist has spent the last two years installing signs at the site.

Jane Mouritz says the tanks are worth preserving. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

Project leader Jane Mouritz said the tanks carried significant historical importance that was worth documenting and preserving.

"They tell a story of some of the hardship that was felt domestically during World War II, when there was fuel rationing and there was fear of invasion," she said.

"That's why it was very important to write the history of these tanks and have it on signage."

Veterans Assist project leader, Jane Mouritz said it was important to write the history of the tanks. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

Inside the tanks, the art stretches up to 20 metres high.

Layers of graffiti transform the cold concrete interiors into immersive chambers of colour and sound.

Ms Mouritz described the experience as "unreal".

"This whole tank is one moving artwork," she said.

"Who would have known, in 1941 when they built tanks to hold fuel, that we would repurpose it in 2026?"

Graffiti gallery

Graffiti artists often work covertly, facing hefty fines and even jail terms if they are caught.

But for them the risk is worth it and the tanks are evidence of their artistic evolution.

There are some remarkable pieces at the site. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

"We first stepped in there about 20 years ago, and there was only one, two, maybe three little pieces in there," Marwick said.

"It was hardly known. It was just left for nature to take over pretty much."

Graffiti is writing or drawings marked on walls or surfaces in public view. (ABC Great Southern: Astrid Volzke)

While the graffiti art is not formally identified as part of the site's recognised cultural heritage significance, the ABC understands the City of Albany has no plans to remove it.

As such, efforts are being made to make the site more accessible, with the Keep Albany Beautiful Committee and Veterans Assist working on building pathways to connect it to nearby public trails.

Marwick hopes that making the site better known, however, will not damage its unique status as a living street art space.

"Because there's nowhere in town that offers any walls, at this stage," he said.

World.title: Police investigate triple fatal crash in Sydney's south
World.content:
Three people have died in a car crash in Sydney’s south, with police attempting to conduct a welfare check at one of the victim’s homes minutes before the incident.

Police attended a home on Second Avenue, Gymea Bay at 12:25am on Saturday following reports of a concern for welfare related to a mental health incident.

A 42-year-old man left the home in a white Audi before officers could speak to him.

Shortly after at 12:30am, emergency services were called to Rocky Point Road at San Souci after reports of a two-car crash.

Police found that the same white Audi had rolled over a concrete barrier before landing on a blue Toyota sedan.

Police say the Audi was travelling at "considerable speed". (ABC News)

The 42-year-old Audi driver died at the scene, as did the driver and passenger of the Toyota.

Investigators have yet to formally identify the occupants of the Toyota.

'Horrific scene'

Superintendent Graham Hibbs said officers believed the Audi was travelling at "considerable speed" when the crash occurred.

"We really feel for the families of all three persons who were involved in this incident and their loved ones," he said.

He said between 20 and 40 bystanders attempted to assist when one of the cars caught fire.

Superintendent Hibbs said first responders would have been met with a "horrific scene".

A crime scene has been established and an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the crash is underway.

A report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: Top End tourism and hospitality businesses seek lifeline amid rising costs
World.content:
Two weeks ago, Flora's Temper — a popular restaurant and bar in the northern Darwin suburb of Nightcliff — announced it was closing down, just two years after opening.

A day later, it shut its doors for good.

The venue's owner, Nicho Peters, isn't looking to blame anyone for the closure.

"It was my business and it was my responsibility to run it right," he said.

Nicho Peters's business Flora's Temper closed its doors this month. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

But the Northern Territory's peak body representing restaurants and bars is less forgiving.

"Flora's Temper had been in planning purgatory for six months, waiting on a permit for outdoor dining," Hospitality NT chief executive Cathy Simmonds said.

" This is Darwin. Why is it so hard to get a permit for outdoor dining? "

A range of challenges

Struggles with obtaining approvals from the City of Darwin are just one challenge facing Top End hospitality and tourism businesses as they head into the peak tourism season, with global fuel shortages pushing up the price of airfares and tightening family holiday budgets.

Michelle and Darren Elliott have scaled back their tourism business to deal with rising costs. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Michelle Elliott has owned and operated the Spirit of Darwin sunset cruise boat alongside her husband Darren for 16 years.

She said the combination of higher fuel costs and a drop in bookings this year had created tough conditions for the business.

"At this time of year we would normally be cruising four to five nights a week with really good numbers, but we've dropped it down to two to three nights a week," she said.

"It's difficult to have enough people to cover your costs if you go out too often."

Looking for solutions

Ms Elliott said her business had not seen a time this difficult since COVID-19, and is calling on the NT government to re-introduce pandemic-era support measures.

"The voucher system that was in during COVID was amazing," she said.

"It got locals out to see what was around in their own backyard, so let's hope they bring something like that back."

Outback workers cut as tourists stay away Skyrocketing fuel prices, as well as concerns around the availability of fuel in remote locations, are causing a 76 per cent loss of revenue for tourist-dependent businesses.

Mr Peters said a voucher scheme could have helped Flora's Temper as well, saying government grants were too focused on bookable tourism experiences, leaving businesses like his to struggle.

"There's a bit of a headwind with a few things going on and any support would be greatly appreciated," he said.

"I take people on croc tours every time they come up here, but there probably needs to be [grants] for when those folks come to town, they want to go to a venue, they want to have a drink, they want to get something to eat.

"There probably needs to be something to help us little guys maintain and improve what we're doing."

While Ms Simmonds is not opposed to vouchers or grant funding in the longer term, she said there were also less expensive measures that could help businesses right away.

Cathy Simmonds is encouraging Territorians to support their local restaurants and cafes as operating costs rise. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"There's a range of solutions that would be good for different small businesses in the hospitality and tourism sectors, and vouchers could definitely play a part there," she said.

"But there's some really easy no- or low-cost things that officials can do right now.

" What we need to hear from council officers and from bureaucrats is a little more yes and a little less no. "

An uncertain future

Any measures introduced now would be too late for Flora's Temper, but Mr Peters wants to see the Darwin council make life easier for other businesses like his.

"A lot of institutions claim to have the back of small business … and they'll talk about wanting to help the little guys," he said.

"Whereas in reality, there's lots of hurdles and lots of red flags and lots of red lights along the way."

Nicho Peters says there are a lot of challenges facing Top End small businesses. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

On the Spirit of Darwin, the tourism season is just getting under way, and so much of the business' success depends on factors outside of Michelle and Darren Elliott's control — but they remain optimistic.

"We made it through COVID, so we can make it through this," Ms Elliott said.

In a statement, the NT Department of Tourism and Hospitality acknowledged fuel pressures and other economic conditions were impacting tourism and hospitality, and that Darwin bookings from May to August had been lower than the same time last year.

The department said in response to the current conditions, it had "significantly increased tactical investment and intervention" in the industry, including by partnering with airlines and launching marketing campaigns.

Asked about vouchers, the department said they "do not necessarily drive interstate visitation or bring new money into the Territory economy", and uptake was "typically concentrated among already popular operators, rather than the businesses experiencing the greatest challenges".

The City of Darwin has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Giant iceberg with shipping containers spotted off Antarctica
World.content:
From the air, they look like seven little ants on a torn piece of white paper.

But a closer inspection of the satellite image reveals something very different.

The "ants" are actually large shipping containers — including one filled with diesel and others packed with rubbish.

And the "white paper" is a huge iceberg, 500 metres long and 300 metres wide.

The containers floated out to sea on the iceberg. (Supplied: ATCM)

Earlier this year, the iceberg and shipping containers were spotted floating off the coast of Antarctica.

How they ended up there — and the environmental consequences of what followed — have been revealed in a report by Antarctic officials from Germany.

"The German government and the AWI (Alfred Wegener Institute) deeply regret the incident and are glad that no-one was injured," the report stated.

There was about an 18-kilometre distance between the iceport, where the containers were, and the German Antarctic station. (Supplied: ATCM)

Ice shelf cracks during severe storm

It all started with the best of intentions.

Germany's Neumayer Station III is located on an ice shelf, about 18 kilometres inland from the sea.

In preparation for the arrival of a vessel that was due to pick up the station's waste, seven shipping containers were positioned a few hundred metres from the icy coastline.

The containers included one with 9,500 litres of Arctic diesel, four with non-hazardous waste, another with a generator and fuel, and one that provided shelter for workers.

At the time, there were no visible signs of crevasses, cracks or fissures in the ice.

But over the next week, between January 13 and 20, a blizzard with winds of 130 kilometres an hour hit the region.

When the conditions finally eased on January 21, an inspection was carried out.

"The logistics team discovered that an iceberg measuring around 500 metres by 300 metres had broken off and drifted into the Weddell Sea," the report said.

" Unfortunately, all of the … containers were on this iceberg. "

The shipping containers belonged to Germany's Neumayer Station III. (Supplied: AWI)

Ship's crew spots iceberg with containers

Germany's Antarctic officials initially considered deploying a plane to search for the missing containers.

But the following day, crew on the German icebreaker RV Polarstern spotted the iceberg and the seven containers.

"The ship immediately ended its scientific investigations [and] travelled to the iceberg, which had drifted … around 140km to the south-east of Neumayer ice port."

Glaciologists were then tasked with assessing whether it would be safe to conduct a retrieval operation.

The iceberg was found to have an overall thickness of 81 metres, including 15 metres above the sea surface.

" The assessment showed that some areas of iceberg were deemed stable enough to allow an exploration team to land on the iceberg. "

Seven shipping containers, including a fuel container, broke away from the ice shelf during a storm. (Supplied: ATCM)

Helicopters were then used to collect almost 1 tonne of equipment, including three drums filled with about 580 litres of Arctic diesel, as well as gas cylinders and batteries.

But that was all that could be salvaged.

"As the risk of the iceberg breaking apart increased, it was impossible to secure more of the cargo without risking human life," the report stated.

" So the salvage attempts were stopped [on January 25] and the remaining material had to remain on the iceberg. "

'Diesel will have leaked'

The last satellite sighting of the iceberg was almost a month later, on February 22.

"It can be assumed that the iceberg has disintegrated shortly afterwards and that the containers have sunk to the seabed," the report stated.

It suggested the four containers with household items and rubbish would have "little direct impact on the ecosystem".

However, the report said the container filled with fuel posed a much bigger risk.

"It can be assumed that it was either damaged by the fall into the sea or imploded on its way to the sea floor.

" In both cases, the diesel will have leaked out. "

The Polar 6 research plane surveyed the iceberg on January 29. (Supplied: ATCM)

The report noted Arctic diesel was lighter and more volatile than heavy fuel oil, meaning it might evaporate more quickly.

But it said Antarctica's low temperatures would slow down any bacterial degradation in the water or sea ice.

"It can therefore be assumed that the fuel will remain in the system for a longer period of time.

" The actual impacts on the ecosystem depend to a large extent on local conditions and therefore cannot be precisely quantified. "

Germany's Antarctic officials said lessons had been learned as a result of the incident.

"In order to further reduce the risk of such a loss of cargo in the future, containers will be stored from now on ... at least 5,000 metres distance to the ice shelf edge."

The report said further glaciological investigations, including ice thickness and consistency, would also be carried out along the route from the Neumayer Station III to the ice port.

World.title: Black mould and broken toilets in 'dismal' government-owned homes
World.content:
Inside one of Australia's most isolated communities, bug infestations, walls covered in black mould and broken toilets are just some of the issues plaguing residents' homes.

When Matilda Djanghara and her two granddaughters need to use the toilet, they're forced to walk down the road.

"I take them to my brother's house, but it's so far," she says.

Kalumburu resident Matilda Djanghara has to walk down the road to use the toilet. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

She says her toilet hasn't worked for weeks.

A towel sits over the drain on her bathroom floor, soaking up water that gushes out if it's flushed.

The plumbing issue means the bathroom and kitchen sinks also pool with water.

Matilda Djanghara has to soak up water that gushes out of the drain on her bathroom floor. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Cupboards and window flyscreens are broken. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

She's one of about 300 people who live in Kalumburu, Western Australia's most northern community.

It was more than 30 degrees and 80 per cent humidity when the ABC visited last month, with Matilda's home offering no reprieve.

She points to an air conditioning unit coated in black dust, saying it has been broken for months.

Matilda Djanghara says the flyscreen doesn't unlock, leaving her worried about the safety of her granddaughters. (ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic)

On her porch, Matilda points to a window, the flyscreen coming up with a pull.

"This window doesn't even shut. There's no safety," she says.

Matilda worries about her granddaughters' health and safety.

Like most houses in Kalumburu, Matilda's is owned by the WA government through the Department of Housing, meaning she can't do the repairs herself.

Matilda Djanghara is worried for the safety of her daughters. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Instead, she must wait for a government contractor to repair any issues.

But getting to Kalumburu isn't easy.

It is only accessible by air for half the year due to flooding, with flights every third day.

Kalumburu is the most northern community in Western Australia. (ABC News)

Despite the issues, Matilda pays rent to live here.

"How are we paying rent when nothing is fixed?" she says.

No hot water

Next door, Kieran Karadada also walks to a relative's house to use the toilet.

When he flushes the toilet or uses the kitchen sink, water floods his floors.

Stagnant brown water sits pooled in the bathroom sink, unable to drain.

Keiran Karadada's blocked bathroom sink does not drain. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"I pay rent and I can't use the toilet," Kieran says.

To make a cup of tea, he walks to the backyard to fill the kettle from an outdoor tap.

He says he has no hot water, making showering in the colder months difficult.

Kieran Karadada says waiting for the department to fix his house is a "headache". (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

He says his living situation has been like this for years, but no-one from the Department has visited his home.

"It's a headache waiting for them," he says.

Rotten floors

Elder Dorothy Djanghara watches her step as she walks on her porch.

The wood has rotted away in multiple places from the heavy rain, leaving jagged holes where floorboards used to be.

Every time it rains at Dorothy's house, the timber deck gets softer and more dangerous. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"Every time the rain comes, it makes the timber soft," she says.

She says her daughter had once fallen "straight through the timber".

The only other way into Dorothy's home is through the back steps, but she says this is even riskier.

Makeshift metal and stone steps balance on two bricks, which wobble beneath her feet.

There is no safe entry into Dorothy Djanghara's house. (ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic)

"The stairs are not safe because of the injuries in my knees," she says.

"I'm so scared of coming up or going down.

Dorothy says it's been this way for over three years.

"[The Department] only take photos, they never did anything."

With children often visiting, she's worried someone might "hurt themselves or break their leg".

Elder Dorothy Djanghara is scared every time she has to leave the house because of her rotten decking. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"We are paying so much money to rent and living in a house like this where there is no help," she says.

Beyond repair

Multiple residents tell the ABC to visit the house with the paperbark tree.

They say it's the "worst" in the community in terms of disrepair.

Kalumburu residents say the "paperbark tree" house is the worst for damage. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Inside, elder Bernadette Waina sits on a couch beside family members seated on a mattress on the floor.

Multiple family members yell at once, pointing to a myriad of issues.

Bernadette Waina says her front door doesn't close properly, leaving enough room for snakes and toads to venture inside. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertogio)

Bernadette walks to her front door, closing a flyscreen that leaves a gap about 10cm wide.

"Snakes and cane toads come in through here," she says.

Bernadette Waina shows how big the gap is when she tries to close her door. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Bernadette Waina doesn't feel safe in her home because her front door cannot close properly. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Stepping outside, the floor is uneven and makeshift installations hold together an air-conditioning unit.

Despite the intense heat in Kalumburu, air conditioning is not a standard inclusion in public housing, meaning many households have made ad hoc installations.

Outside Bernadette Waina's house, the floor is uneven and makeshift installations hold up her air-conditioning unit. (ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic )

While the ABC visits, a worker approaches Bernadette's front door.

"It's the housing mob," her son yells out.

A worker's hand comes through the flyscreen and replaces a small fan switch dial.

He doesn't step inside, and says he has 30 jobs on his list but this is his only one for Bernadette's house.

A Department of Housing worker comes to Bernadette's house to fix the fan switch, but nothing else. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

When the ABC asks why he doesn't stay longer to complete more repairs, he says plane capacity is limited and Kalumburu is "not a great place to stay".

Bernadette shakes her head in anger, saying the Department often sends maintenance workers for "a couple of hours", meaning critical jobs are left unfinished.

"How much is the government spending on a charter plane?" she says.

"They do things in a hurry, and we still got problems."

The Department of Housing and Works did not respond to questions on how much it spends to charter a plane to Kalumburu.

Bernadette Waina and her daughter, Natasha Waina. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Bernadette doesn't hold back, saying the process has her feeling "pissed off".

"It's not right. They live in luxury, in good homes. We might as well go live in a cave," she says.

Bug infestation

Bernadette walks the ABC to her daughter Natasha Waina's house.

Bernadette and Natasha Waina walk down a semi-flooded road in Kalumburu. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Inside, the kitchen sink has food sitting in stagnant water.

"I had it [like this] for two years, it's been blocked," Natasha says.

She says she told the Department, but workers only came for a couple of hours and hadn't fixed it properly.

"I used it again and it blocked," she says.

Natasha Waina says she has to walk to the outside tap to make a tea. (ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic)

Natasha walks to the laundry sink or outside tap whenever she needs water.

Black mould coats the doors, walls and the floor inside her bathroom.

Black mould coats the walls and floors of Natasha Waina's home. (ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic)

An empty air conditioning wall cavity is stuffed with clothing and furniture, in an attempt to keep bugs out.

Inside, pests cover the walls, coating the faces of religious statues.

Broken locks

Inside Charmaine Djanghara's house, a deep freezer is pulled against her entry door.

Charmaine says she uses it as a safety mechanism, because her front door and flyscreen haven't locked since last year.

Charmaine Djanghara moves a deep freezer in front of the door to make her home safe. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"I keep reporting and reporting and nothing is done," she said.

The single parent of three says she worries about the safety of her children, saying they haven't had hot water for at least three years.

Charmaine Djanghara says her home has not had hot water for three years. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"I just want to keep them safe and live in a better home," Charmaine says.

"I am losing hope."

Falling through the cracks

Tenants must report maintenance issues with the department by phone.

But in Kalumburu, phone and internet reception often cuts out.

For many residents, English is not their first language and some cannot read or write.

People say reports have fallen through the cracks, with some blaming the current Kalumburu Aboriginal Corporation (KAC) or previous leadership.

Kalumburu residents have been calling on the Department of Housing to do more frequent inspections. (ABC Giulia Bertoglio)

Despite this, residents have called on the department to do more frequent inspections.

According to the department's policy, it must conduct up to four inspections each year to identify maintenance issues and arrange required repairs.

KAC chief executive Kim Holm says this hasn't been happening.

"If they were here six-monthly or 12-monthly … people would have that opportunity [to raise issues]," she says.

Having worked in remote locations around the country, Kim says nothing compares to Kalumburu.

Kim Holm says some of the government-owned homes are in dismal condition. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"This is the absolute worst I have seen," she says.

"It's just dismal."

"[The department] … have not respected the human beings living here and I'm really disappointed."

Kim would like to see a different approach.

"When they come, they fix one or two minor things, they don't look at the bigger picture," she says.

"Rather than flying someone in for a day, fly someone in for a week, get the jobs done and fly them out again."

Late last year, Aboriginal Community Housing Limited, which manages inspections in Kalumburu on behalf of the department, visited most houses in the community to document issues.

While Kim says she received confirmation the report had been submitted to the department, "nothing has happened since".

"We're still sitting here waiting with derelict houses and people living in absolutely poor conditions," she says.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Department of Housing and Works said it endeavoured to respond to all maintenance requests in "a timely manner".

"However factors such as extreme weather events, remoteness and an inability to access tenancies may cause delays," the spokesperson said.

"Road access to Kalumburu has been significantly restricted due to serious cyclone activity, however DHW actively works to clear any maintenance backlogs.

"DHW has been working to address maintenance concerns in Kalumburu, and contractors are scheduled to return to Kalumburu in the coming weeks."

The department did not respond to questions on the average cost associated with sending contractors to Kalumburu.

World.title: ‘Wallabies is the end goal’: Pritchard brothers’ dream alive despite PNG Chiefs meeting
World.content:
SportRugby UnionPNG ‘Wallabies is the end goal’: Pritchard brothers’ dream alive despite PNG Chiefs meeting Jonathan Drennan May 23, 2026 — 9:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brumbies centre Kadin Pritchard has left the door open to a potential NRL switch to the PNG Chiefs, but says he and his brother Treyvon have plenty of unfinished business in rugby. After playing a key role in defeating the Waratahs in Sydney, Pritchard said representing the Wallabies alongside Treyvon, who plays for the Reds, was a dream that he is determined to achieve. High-flying Brumbies back Kadin Pritchard is in demand. Getty Images The brothers are contracted to Super Rugby until the end of the 2027 season, with Kadin saying it remains his focus, regardless of meeting the PNG Chiefs in Brisbane last Tuesday. “Obviously, the Wallabies is the end goal, that’s the international stage. I think everyone strives for that, if you’re not striving for that, then why are you really playing?



“Obviously, the chance to play with my brother, I think that would be a super special moment. He’s doing his thing, and I’m doing my thing and potentially, hopefully, that dream can come true. It’s something we’ve talked about as kids growing up.” Pritchard has started 12 games at outside centre for the Brumbies. Treyvon will start his second game of the season for the Reds on Saturday against Moana Pasifika in New Zealand. Treyvon Pritchard scores his first Super Rugby try for Queensland. Getty Images “I think we’ve still got the season ahead of us, and my focus is rugby at the moment, and then trying to pull the Brums over the line here, and whatever happens in the future happens in the future,” Pritchard said. “Potentially, I’m open to trying stuff (in the NRL), but like I said, my focus is rugby as long as I’m contracted, which is also next year. So my focus is just sticking to rugby union and trying to be the best that I can be on the field for the Brumbies.”



Related Article Australian rugby Half the battle: What Australian rugby can learn from Matt the Bat and Mr Cricket Pritchard refers to his brother as “probably my best mate” and revealed that, growing up, Treyvon pretended to be New Zealand Test star Damian McKenzie while he idolised his All Blacks teammate Will Jordan in backyard games at home in Brisbane. Both the Brumbies and the Reds are on course for Super Rugby finals, and while the Pritchard brothers rarely discuss rugby together, it’s a different story for their parents, Dan and Brenda. “We have the split jerseys there at home, so they try and not choose a side, I think. Mum’s pretty funny, she goes for the winning team, whoever’s winning,” Pritchard said. “And then she said, ‘Oh, I’m not a Brumbies fan any more’ and then goes for Reds, but then we won this week. So she texted me, ‘oh, I’m back on the Brumbies’ bandwagon again’. So then whoever’s doing well, the parents just blow through and obviously give us positive reinforcement.”



Pritchard also credits his parents for helping him and his brother deal with the intense scrutiny that has been focused on them as two of rugby’s premier young talents. “Mum and Dad kind of instilled in us just to be grateful for the opportunities that we’ve been given, knowing that at any time it can be taken away,” Pritchard said. “We’ve been taught to be grounded and be humble and knowing that God has given us an opportunity, so we need to take it with both hands, but at the same time, like, it’s not there forever and it can be taken away at any minute.” Watch every match of Super Rugby Pacific live and exclusive on Stan Sport.
